# How Perseús got its accent back

The ASCII form *perseus* is missing something. **Perseús** restores the ​marks the source language used to distinguish this name from a thousand others — and those marks change how the name is read, pronounced, and understood. This post explains, with the full ‌scholarly record behind it, what each restored mark preserves: the Greek evidence, the reconstructed sound, the myths the name carries, and the mechanical logic of what each restored mark preserves. By the end, ‌the marks in Perseús will look less like ornaments and more like what they are — recovered evidence, pinned back in its proper place.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Perseús
- **ASCII form:** ​perseus
- **Meaning:** "Destroyer, possibly Persian"
- **Domain of influence:** Hero, Slayer of Medousa
- **Pantheon:** Greek
- **Restoration:** Preserves stress
- **Original script:** Περσεύς (Greek)

## Overview

**Perseus** (*perseus*) — Hero, Slayer of Medousa · Destroyer, possibly Persian ​— belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Hero, Slayer of Medousa". The name means "Destroyer, possibly Persian".

**Perseus** is hero, slayer of medousa. The name means "Destroyer, ​possibly Persian" and belongs to the greek tradition.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Perseus** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/perseus/). The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one ​historically valid Unicode restoration exists. The plain ASCII form *perseus* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as ​philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Greek as **Περσεύς**. Etymologically it means "Destroyer, possibly Persian".

The ASCII form *perseus* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry ‌diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Perseus** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The original carries both stress ​and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists.

## Mythology

The stories of Perseus place hero, slayer of medousa at the center of ​a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

Perseus appears in greek tradition as hero, slayer of medousa. The name's meaning, "Destroyer, possibly Persian", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory ​(Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Perseus in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Perseus survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each ​version reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The ​restoration Perseus gives the figure a stable name around which these variants orbit.

### The Shower of Gold (The Birth)

Akrisios, king of Argos, went to Delphi to ask the oracle for a ​son and received instead a death sentence: his daughter Danaë would bear a child who would kill him. He locked Danaë in a brazen chamber sunk underground, but Zeus came upon her as ‌a shower of gold — 'she took the gold into her lap,' as Simonides sang (PMG 543) — passing through bronze with an immortal's ease. When Perseus was born, Akrisios would not ​kill mother and child outright; he had them sealed in a chest and cast into the sea, which carried them gently to the island of Seriphos. There the fisherman Diktys drew them ashore ‌and gave them his house (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.2.1; cf. Pindar, Pythian 12.12–16). The oracle has already framed the whole of the hero's life: his greatness and his grandfather's death are the same ​event, waiting years away at a games-ground for a discus to close the circle.

### The Graiai and the Gear (The Quest)

Polydectes, king of Seriphos, desired Danaë and wanted Perseus gone. Feigning a ‌bride-price for Hippodameia, he demanded horses of his whole court; Perseus rashly promised the Gorgon's head instead — and Polydectes held him to it (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.2.3). Athena and Hermes took charge of ​the impossible errand and led him first to the Graiai, the 'grey ones' who from birth were old women, sisters of the Gorgons, sharing a single eye and a single tooth (Hesiod, ‌Theogony 270–273). Perseus snatched the eye as it passed from face to face and ransomed it for the road to the nymphs; from them he received the kibisis that safely holds the head, ​the cap of Hades that makes its wearer unseen, and winged sandals; from Hermes the adamantine harpe, from Athena the polished bronze shield (Apollodorus 2.2.3–4; Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.610ff). The quest's real lesson ‌is assembled before the monster is met: this hero wins not by native strength but by holding hostage what others cannot do without — an eye, a tooth, and the world's best equipment.

### ​The Head of Medousa (The Slaying)

Beyond Ocean lay the Gorgons, winged women with brazen claws and serpent hair; of the three sisters, only Medousa was mortal (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.2.4). Perseus came ​upon them sleeping and, watching Medousa's image in the mirror-bright shield rather than the living face, struck once with the harpe. The neck opened and from it sprang **Pegasus** and the warrior **Chrysaor** ‌— 'when Perseus cut off her head, great Chrysaor and the horse Pegasus sprang forth' (Hesiod, Theogony 280–286). The sleeping sisters woke and took the wing in pursuit, but the cap of Hades ‌hid him, and he was gone into the air. The gods had not sent him to punish Medousa so much as to harvest her: from the monster's death leap the winged horse ‌that will carry Zeus's thunderbolts and the father of the monster Geryon — terror and poetry born from a single stroke of the sickle-sword.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Perseus concentrates ​in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Name** — The restored form Perseus, carrying scholarly and cultural weight.
- **Domain** — Hero, Slayer of Medousa

Symbols ​function as a visual shorthand: they allow devotees and artists to recognize Perseus across media and centuries. The attributes listed above are not decorative; each one encodes a claim about power, identity, or ‌function. The restored spelling Perseus carries the same precision in textual form.

Vase painting, sculpture, and votive reliefs disseminate the visual identity of Perseus. Artists returned to attributes such as Name, Domain, ​creating a recognizable iconographic shorthand.

The restored spelling Perseus reproduces in text the same precision that painters sought in image. Each attribute encodes a claim about power, identity, or function.

- **Harpe (adamantine sickle-sword)** ​— The curved blade Hermes gave him for the one stroke at Medousa's neck — a weapon older than the gods' order
- **Mirrored shield** — Athena's polished bronze, in which Perseus watched the ‌Gorgon safely — knowledge taken only by reflection
- **Cap of Hades** — The helmet of invisibility that hid him from the waking Gorgon sisters and the giants of Seriphos
- **Kibisis** — The ​wallet that holds the severed head without harm — the first container built for a monster
- **Gorgoneion** — The apotropaic face itself, set on Athena's aegis, turning enemies to stone at the city's ​threshold

## Epithets & Cult Titles

Greek gods and heroes accumulate epithets — cultic titles that specify place, function, or quality. For Perseus, the tradition preserves epithets that stress hero.

Epicleses connected with ‌Name, Domain sharpen the name for local worship and literary invocation. The restored form Perseus carries the same vowel quantities that these epithets inherited in oral performance.

## The Homeric Hymns

The Homeric Hymns, ​a collection of ancient Greek hexameter poems, include invocations and narratives that shape the reception of Perseus. While Perseus does not always receive a separate, surviving hymn, the figure appears in the ‌broader epic and hymnic environment that celebrates the Olympian order.

The hymns map divine genealogy, power, and cultic honor, and Perseus's role as hero places the name within that hexameter world. The PuniCodex ​restoration Perseus preserves the prosodic features that rhapsodes would have articulated.

## Oracle Sites & Sanctuaries

Sanctuaries and oracular centers anchored the cult of Perseus in the Greek landscape. Major sites include locations ​where the domain of hero was ritually honored.

Pilgrims, offerings, and festival calendars tied the name to specific topography. The restoration Perseus gives the figure a stable address in the digital landscape analogous ​to those ancient centers.

## Archaeology & Evidence

No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet assigned to Perseus with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Greek ​name of this type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it ‌would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming Περσεύς, sanctuary or cult remains tied to hero and iconography matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against the ‌reconstructed form of the name before entering the scholarly record.

## Realm & Domain

**Perseus** is hero, slayer of medousa. The name means "Destroyer, possibly Persian" and belongs to the greek tradition.

### Sacred ​Name

The restoration Perseus returns the figure to scholarly recognition.

### Hero

Central domain: hero, slayer of medousa.

### Living Tradition

Honored in greek myth, cult, and cultural memory.

### Unicode Restoration

Preserved as a flagship ‌temple despite the unregistrable plain-ASCII form.

### The Gorgon-Slayer

With Athena's mirrored shield and Hermes' adamantine harpe he took the one head no god dared face — Medousa's.

### Divine Favor

Athena and Hermes ​equip him; the kibisis holds the head; winged sandals and the cap of Hades carry him beyond Ocean.

### Founder of Mycenae

From his dynasty — Electryon, Sthenelus, Eurystheus — come Heracles and the ​Argive royal line.

## A Meditation

To contemplate Perseus is to hold the idea of hero, Slayer of Medousa in the mind and to ask what of it endures. The name means "Destroyer, ​possibly Persian" — and a name that carries its meaning so openly invites meditation rather than mere recollection. The tradition remembers the name as hero, Slayer of Medousa · Destroyer, possibly Persian.

Sit ​with the restored form — Perseus — and the diacritics themselves become the practice: each mark is a small act of attention, a refusal to let the plain ASCII form *perseus* stand ​in for the whole. What the tradition preserved in this name, the restoration asks the reader to preserve in turn.
